questions.stem: A woman experiences a post-partum haemorrhage associated with uterine atony that is unresponsive to oxytocin and ergometrine. The recommended intramuscular dose of carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha ) to be administered is

opts.why: 150 µg is below the standard 250 µg adult intramuscular carboprost dose.
100 µg underdoses the usual adult prostaglandin F₂α regimen.
500 µg is twice the recommended single IM dose and increases prostaglandin adverse effects.

questions.expl: The standard adult carboprost dose for atonic postpartum haemorrhage is 250 micrograms IM or intramyometrially, repeatable according to protocol. It can cause bronchospasm and warrants particular caution or avoidance in asthma.
questions.note: Historical reconstruction: the recalled Anki scenario mentioned asthma, but the official stem did not.

questions.stem: A 74-year old man in the post-anaesthesia care unit complains of chest pain. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed. The occluded coronary artery is the

opts.why: LAD occlusion more typically produces anterior V1–V4 ST changes, not the reconstructed inferior pattern.
A diagonal-branch infarct generally produces anterolateral rather than inferior territory changes.
Left main occlusion causes widespread ischaemic patterns, not the isolated inferior ECG described.

questions.expl: The reconstructed inferior-ST-elevation ECG shows greater elevation in lead III than II with reciprocal changes, favouring right coronary artery occlusion. LAD and diagonal branches more often cause anterior or lateral changes. A dominant circumflex can also cause an inferior infarction.
questions.note: An ECG representative of the recalled RCA culprit is supplied for practice; the ANZCA ECG was not published.

questions.stem: Techniques to improve the speed of onset and spread of a peribulbar block include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Gentle digital pressure is an accepted adjunct to support peribulbar spread when applied appropriately.
Hyaluronidase helps local anaesthetic diffuse through orbital connective tissues.
Controlled Honan balloon compression can help distribution without the trauma of forceful massage.

questions.expl: Hyaluronidase improves diffusion of local anaesthetic; gentle external pressure may reduce chemosis and improve spread. Forceful ocular massage risks dangerously increasing intraocular pressure and is not recommended.

questions.stem: An adult with renal failure on regular haemodialysis has an ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical status classification of at least

opts.why: ASA I requires an otherwise healthy patient, which established dialysis-dependent renal disease is not.
ASA II describes mild systemic disease, below the severity of stable ESRD requiring dialysis.
ASA IV denotes severe disease that is a constant threat to life, not all stable dialysis patients.

questions.expl: Stable end-stage kidney disease requiring regular dialysis is an ASA III example. ASA IV requires severe systemic disease posing a constant threat to life, such as acute renal failure or uncontrolled complications.

questions.stem: The breast does NOT receive sensory innervation from the

opts.t: Anterior and lateral intercostal cutaneous branches
opts.why: Anterior/lateral intercostal cutaneous branches provide the main breast cutaneous sensory supply.
The intercostobrachial nerve (T2 lateral cutaneous) supplies the axillary tail/adjacent region.
Supraclavicular fibres contribute to upper breast skin sensation.

questions.expl: The breast and overlying skin are supplied chiefly by anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves T2–T6, with superior clavicular contributions. Posterior branches mainly supply the back and are not the primary breast cutaneous innervation.
questions.note: The source question is anatomically broad; reconstructed option distinguishes dorsal from ventral intercostal branches.

questions.stem: A derived value from an arterial blood gas sample is

opts.why: PH is directly measured with a hydrogen-ion-selective electrode on the blood-gas analyser.
PaCO₂ is measured by a carbon dioxide-sensitive electrode rather than calculated from pH.
PaO₂ is measured with an oxygen electrode rather than calculated from other results.

questions.expl: In standard blood-gas analysis, pH, PaCO₂ and PaO₂ are measured by electrodes. Bicarbonate is calculated using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation unless separately assayed by a chemistry analyser.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a serum sodium of 110 mmol/L. A feature NOT consistent with a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antiduretic hormone (SIADH) is

opts.why: SIADH typically presents as clinically euvolaemic hyponatraemia.
Urinary sodium above 30 is consistent with non-hypovolaemic sodium handling in SIADH.
Hypotonic serum is expected when SIADH causes water retention.

questions.expl: SIADH requires inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypotonic plasma; very dilute urine (below 100 mOsm/kg) implies appropriate ADH suppression, not typical SIADH. Euvolaemia, hypotonic hyponatraemia and urinary sodium elevation are expected.

questions.stem: Identified risk factors for opioid-induced ventilatory impairment DO NOT include

opts.t: Antidepressant use alone, without sedative co-medication

opts.why: Increasing age is associated with reduced ventilatory reserve and higher opioid sensitivity.
OSA predisposes to upper-airway obstruction and nocturnal opioid-related hypoventilation.
Renal dysfunction can increase exposure to renally cleared opioids and active metabolites.

questions.expl: Established risk factors for opioid-induced ventilatory impairment include OSA, increasing age, renal dysfunction, obesity, and sedative coadministration. Antidepressant use by itself is not the usual independent risk factor in the recalled list.
questions.note: Some sedating antidepressants or combinations with opioids can still increase risk; this is a period-specific reconstructed exception.

questions.stem: Risks associated with robot-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy surgery in comparison with open prostatectomy include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.t: Higher risk of obturator nerve injury
Longer operating time and steep Trendelenburg
opts.why: Prolonged Trendelenburg/pneumoperitoneum are characteristic robotic exposure risks.
Head-down position promotes facial and conjunctival oedema.
Steep positioning and prolonged lithotomy can produce compression neuropathies.

questions.expl: Robotic prostatectomy has risks arising from steep Trendelenburg, positioning and pneumoperitoneum. The recalled exception was an increased obturator nerve injury risk compared with open procedures; pelvic nodal dissection can still injure the nerve in either approach.
questions.note: Comparative risks depend on surgical technique and experience; reconstructed recalled answer.

questions.stem: The most likely complication from ultrasound guided left internal jugular central venous line insertion is

opts.why: Air embolism is possible but less frequent than uncomplicated arterial puncture with ultrasound IJV access.
Carotid pseudoaneurysm is a rarer sequela of major vessel injury.
Chylothorax is rare and related to thoracic-duct injury, especially at the left neck base.

questions.expl: Arterial puncture remains among the more frequent mechanical complications of internal-jugular catheterisation even with ultrasound. The other events are recognised but generally less frequent.

questions.stem: Benzatropine ameliorates the side effects of drugs that antagonise

opts.why: Blocking muscarinic receptors is benzatropine's action, not the original drug effect it counteracts.
5-HT₃ antagonism primarily produces antiemetic effects, not acute dystonia.
H₁ antagonism generally causes sedation, not D₂-associated extrapyramidal symptoms.

questions.expl: Benzatropine is antimuscarinic and treats drug-induced parkinsonism or acute dystonia from dopamine D₂ blockade. It does not specifically reverse H₁, 5-HT₃ or M₁ receptor blockade.

questions.stem: Regarding healthcare research, the PICO framework describes

opts.why: The P stands for Population/Problem, not prevalence; C denotes comparator, not cost.
Investigation/causation/observation are not the standard PICO elements.
Incidence, confidence and odds are epidemiological measures, not the framework components.

questions.expl: PICO is the framework for constructing answerable clinical research questions: population or problem, intervention, comparison and outcome.

questions.stem: The drug of choice for the treatment of duct dependent congenital heart disease is

opts.why: Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandins and promotes PDA closure, opposite to ductal maintenance.
Ibuprofen also closes a patent ductus by prostaglandin inhibition.
Carboprost is a uterotonic prostaglandin used for haemorrhage, not neonatal ductal patency.

questions.expl: Alprostadil maintains ductus arteriosus patency in duct-dependent congenital heart disease. Indomethacin and ibuprofen promote ductal closure; carboprost is a uterotonic rather than a ductal-maintaining agent.

questions.stem: A patient has blunt chest trauma. A thoracotomy is indicated if the immediate blood drainage after closed thoracostomy is greater than

opts.why: 500 mL is below the immediate-output threshold specified by the cited ANZCOR guidance.
2,500 mL would delay referral until far beyond the guideline threshold.
250 mL is insufficient as a stand-alone massive haemothorax indication for thoracotomy.

questions.expl: The relevant ANZCOR trauma guideline recommends surgical exploration after more than 1 L immediate output or ongoing drainage over 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours. Other trauma guidelines use 1.5 L as a separate threshold, so specify the source.
questions.note: Period-specific ANZCOR threshold differs from some ATLS/trauma references.

questions.stem: A factor that is NOT used to calculate the Child-Pugh score is

opts.why: Albumin is one of the five Child–Pugh domains.
INR or prothrombin time measures hepatic synthetic function within Child–Pugh.
Clinical encephalopathy severity contributes directly to the score.

questions.expl: Child–Pugh scoring comprises bilirubin, albumin, INR or prothrombin time, ascites and encephalopathy. Serum sodium is used in MELD-Na, not Child–Pugh.

questions.stem: The relatively slower onset of action of bupivacaine with adrenaline in brachial plexus anaesthesia compared to other local anaesthetics relates to

opts.why: Adrenaline reduces systemic absorption and does not explain bupivacaine's intrinsically slow nerve entry.
Aqueous solubility alone is not the main determinant of non-ionised diffusion through nerves.
Bupivacaine is highly protein bound, not weakly bound; protein binding largely affects duration.

opts.t: Relatively high pKa and a lower unionised fraction at physiological pH

questions.expl: Local anaesthetic onset is influenced by pKa: agents more ionised at physiological pH enter nerves more slowly. Bupivacaine has pKa near 8.1; concentration and local tissue factors also affect onset. Lipid solubility primarily affects potency, and protein binding duration.
questions.note: Recalled answers conflict: one Anki card said high lipid solubility, while a 21.2-specific Brainscape card keys pKa. This item follows standard pharmacology.

questions.stem: You administer a dose of intravenous indocyanine green to facilitate videoangiography during cerebral aneurysm surgery. The changes in pulse oximetry (SpO2) and cerebral oxygen tissue saturation (SctO2) you expect to see on your monitors are

opts.why: ICG usually creates an apparent fall in pulse-oximeter reading, not a rise.
Cerebral NIRS may rise rather than fall because of differential wavelength absorption.

opts.t: SpO₂ falls transiently while cerebral NIRS saturation rises

opts.why: An SpO₂ rise is not the characteristic temporary optical artefact of indocyanine green.

questions.expl: Indocyanine green can alter optical absorption at the wavelengths used by pulse oximetry and cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy, producing apparent decreased SpO₂ and increased cerebral tissue saturation. These are measurement artefacts, not necessarily physiological changes.

questions.stem: The CRASH-2 trial showed tranexamic acid administration to trauma victims results in a reduction in

opts.t: All-cause mortality from every cause in all subgroups
opts.why: The all-cause mortality benefit was demonstrated in the trial overall, but the unqualified 'every cause in all subgroups' claim is too broad.
CRASH-2 did not show a significant decrease in transfusion requirement.
Pulmonary embolism incidence was not reduced by TXA; the benefit was haemorrhagic death.

opts.t: Death due to bleeding following trauma

questions.expl: CRASH-2 showed early TXA reduces death due to bleeding, particularly when given within three hours. Overall mortality also decreased in the trial, but blood-product use did not fall significantly and the primary benefit is bleeding mortality.

questions.stem: An awake patient in the post-anaesthesia care unit complains of breathlessness. The FiO2 is 0.4 via a facemask. An arterial blood gas taken at the time shows PaO2 135 mmHg, PaCO2 48 mmHg, and SpO2 100% The alveolar-arterial gradient (in mmHg) is approximately

opts.why: Fifty is too small; the alveolar oxygen tension is about 225 mmHg, leaving a 90-mmHg gradient.
Twenty substantially underestimates the 225−135 mmHg alveolar–arterial difference.
One hundred and fifty would require PAO₂ about 285 mmHg, ignoring CO₂ subtraction from inspired oxygen tension.

questions.expl: On room pressure at sea level, PAO₂ ≈ 0.4 × (760−47) − 48/0.8 = 225 mmHg. The A–a difference is about 225 − 135 = 90 mmHg. Assumes standard barometric pressure and respiratory quotient 0.8.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman has a recent onset of dyspnoea and undergoes a right heart catheterisation, with results displayed below. Her pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 10 mmHg. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Mitral regurgitation causing pulmonary hypertension usually increases wedge/left atrial pressure.
Mitral stenosis characteristically raises PCWP, unlike the 10-mmHg wedge given.
Aortic stenosis with pulmonary hypertension is a post-capillary left-heart process, not normal wedge pressure.

questions.expl: A raised pulmonary artery pressure with normal wedge pressure and characteristic right-heart pressure changes suggests precapillary pulmonary hypertension from PE rather than elevated left-sided filling pressure. Mitral disease commonly elevates PCWP.
questions.note: The original right-heart-catheter diagram/results were not published. A labelled representative pressure-trace figure is provided for this recalled diagnosis.
questions.imgcap: Recalled Anki study image — not authenticated as the original ANZCA figure

questions.stem: A ten-year-old boy (weight 30 kg) has a displaced distal forearm fracture that requires manipulation and application of plaster. The volume of 0.5% lidocaine (lignocaine) that should be used for intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block) is

opts.why: 60 mL of 0.5% delivers 300 mg lidocaine, 10 mg/kg, excessive for this child.
Six mL gives 30 mg and insufficient vascular-compartment filling for a 30-kg IVRA.
Thirty-six mL delivers 180 mg, twice the recalled 3-mg/kg protocol.

questions.expl: A commonly recalled paediatric Bier-block protocol uses 0.6 mL/kg of 0.5% lidocaine, giving 18 mL for 30 kg (90 mg, 3 mg/kg). Local protocols vary; tourniquet safety and maximum dose are critical.
questions.note: Do not assume this volume applies universally to paediatric IVRA; consult local protocol.

questions.stem: A five-year-old child weighing 25 kg is to be strictly nil by mouth overnight following a laparotomy. The most appropriate fluid prescription is

opts.why: Hypotonic 0.18% saline raises the risk of hospital-acquired hyponatraemia under postoperative ADH secretion.

opts.t: Isotonic crystalloid containing 5% glucose at an appropriately reduced maintenance rate

opts.why: Plain free water has no sodium and is unsafe as IV maintenance fluid.

opts.t: Isotonic saline 200 mL/h as routine maintenance
opts.why: 200 mL/h greatly exceeds the calculated 25-kg maintenance rate of roughly 65 mL/h.

questions.expl: Children after major surgery are vulnerable to non-osmotic ADH secretion and hyponatraemia. Isotonic maintenance fluid with glucose is preferred, often at reduced rate if fluid retention risk is high. Full 4–2–1 calculation for 25 kg is 65 mL/h before individualisation.
questions.note: The exact rate and clinical context were not in the official stem; sample regimen is reconstructed.

questions.stem: Of the following, the lifestyle modification that is least effective in reducing essential hypertension is

opts.why: Reducing dietary sodium lowers BP and has trial support.
Regular exercise lowers resting blood pressure.
Weight loss helps lower blood pressure where excess body weight exists.

questions.expl: Potassium-rich diets generally lower BP; deliberately reducing dietary potassium is not an effective antihypertensive measure and may raise BP. Exercise, sodium reduction and weight loss reduce pressure.

questions.stem: Sensory innervation of the cornea is by the

opts.why: CN II is sensory for sight, not corneal touch or the afferent blink reflex.

opts.t: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V₁)

opts.why: CN VII closes the eyelid (efferent blink), not the sensory afferent limb.
CN III controls ocular movement/pupil responses, not corneal sensation.

questions.expl: The corneal afferent limb is via long ciliary nerves from nasociliary V₁. VII mediates the efferent blink; II serves vision and III extraocular movement/pupillary response.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male has continued post operative bleeding after an extraction of an impacted third molar tooth under a general anaesthetic. The patient mentions that his father bruises quite easily. His coagulation screen reveals: (Coagulation tests provided). The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Haemophilia B is usually X-linked factor IX deficiency with haemarthroses/deep bleeding; the mucosal family pattern favours VWD.
ITP generally presents with thrombocytopenia and is less likely to show the described inherited pattern.
Factor VII deficiency chiefly prolongs PT; primary mucosal bleeding with normal PT suggests VWD instead.

questions.expl: Mucosal bleeding after dental extraction and a first-degree family history suggest an inherited primary-haemostasis defect, especially von Willebrand disease. Normal or mildly prolonged aPTT can occur; confirm with vWF antigen/activity and factor VIII assays.
questions.note: The original coagulation values were omitted. This is the likely recall, not an independently established diagnosis from the official stem alone.

questions.stem: The condition in which volatile anaesthesia is least appropriate is

opts.why: Stable renal impairment does not by itself make every volatile agent contraindicated.
Volatiles can be useful bronchodilators in controlled asthma and are not inherently prohibited.
A remote uncomplicated MI requires risk evaluation but does not impose a universal volatile-agent ban.

questions.expl: Volatile anaesthetics can trigger anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis and potentially fatal hyperkalaemia in dystrophinopathies; a non-triggering technique is generally chosen. The other conditions do not universally prohibit volatiles.
questions.note: Reconstructed response; the original answer options were not published.

questions.stem: International guidelines state that patients presenting for major surgery have inadequate or low iron stores if their serum ferritin level is less than

opts.why: 500 µg/L is much higher than the absolute iron-deficiency cut-off and would overdiagnose deficiency.
200 µg/L is not the routine absolute ferritin threshold in the absence of inflammatory context.

opts.t: Ferritin below 300 micrograms/L regardless of inflammation
opts.why: 300 µg/L alone does not define iron deficiency regardless of inflammation.

questions.expl: Consensus definitions of absolute iron deficiency use ferritin under 30 µg/L. In inflammation, ferritin may be falsely high, and iron deficiency can be diagnosed with ferritin below 100 µg/L or reduced transferrin saturation in appropriate contexts.

questions.stem: Globe perforation during eye block is more common in myopic eyes because the

opts.t: Increased axial length of a highly myopic globe

opts.why: High myopia is associated with thin vulnerable posterior sclera/staphyloma, not protective thickening.
Vessel density is not the anatomical reason that a long myopic globe is easily perforated.
High myopia lengthens the globe; a shortened AP diameter is the opposite anatomical change.

questions.expl: Highly myopic eyes have increased axial length and often a posterior staphyloma, increasing the chance that a regional ophthalmic needle perforates the globe.

questions.stem: A drug which is likely to slow the heart rate in a patient with a heart transplant is

opts.why: Atropine works chiefly via vagal blockade, ineffective on a denervated transplanted sinus node.
Digoxin's major nodal slowing is vagally mediated, so it is often ineffective in the transplanted heart.
Glycopyrrolate is antimuscarinic and lacks the direct beta-blocking mechanism of esmolol.

questions.expl: Esmolol acts directly on cardiac beta receptors and can slow the denervated transplanted heart. Atropine and glycopyrrolate depend on vagal pathways; digoxin is usually ineffective for sinus-node slowing in a denervated heart.
questions.note: A second recall option set included adenosine, which can produce marked bradycardia in transplanted hearts; this reconstructed version uses the clearer first option set.

questions.stem: A patient requiring an elective major joint replacement has had a recent stroke. The minimum recommended duration between the stroke and surgery is

opts.why: One month is shorter than the contemporaneous AHA/ASA recommended minimum following stroke.

opts.t: At least six months after a recent ischaemic stroke

opts.why: Two weeks is far too soon for elective major joint surgery after recent stroke.
Six years is neither a guideline threshold nor a clinically necessary delay.

questions.expl: The 2021 AHA/ASA perioperative statement advised delaying elective surgery at least six months after stroke and preferably nine months. Some recalled banks simply key nine months; the word minimum makes six months the more precise historical answer.
questions.note: Historical recommendations have subsequently changed. This version distinguishes minimum from preferred delay.

questions.stem: High-risk transthoracic echocardiogram findings associated with aortic dissection include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.t: Isolated systemic hypertension without direct evidence of dissection
Visible intimal flap in the thoracic aorta
opts.why: A visible intimal flap is direct echocardiographic evidence of aortic dissection.
Aortic-root enlargement supports possible proximal aortic pathology.
A new effusion may signal haemopericardium from proximal dissection/rupture.

questions.expl: High-risk echocardiographic findings of dissection include an intimal flap, aortic root enlargement, severe new aortic regurgitation or tamponade. Hypertension is a risk factor, not a specific echocardiographic sign.
questions.note: Original recalled options missing. Representative reconstruction uses a non-imaging risk factor as the exception.

questions.stem: You are involved in the care of a two-year-old child who ingested a button battery within the last 4 hours. You should consider giving

opts.why: Activated charcoal does not bind a battery or prevent local electrochemical oesophageal injury.

opts.t: Sucralfate orally while arranging urgent endoscopic retrieval

opts.why: Observation can allow serious battery injury within hours and is unsafe if the battery is in the oesophagus.
Induced emesis increases aspiration and re-exposure risk and delays urgent removal.

questions.expl: For a child older than one year with recent suspected oesophageal button-battery ingestion, honey before hospital and sucralfate in hospital may reduce injury while urgent removal is arranged. Do not delay endoscopy for medication.
questions.note: Protocol eligibility and dose vary by age and timing; period-specific recalled answer is sucralfate.

questions.stem: Stellate ganglion block is NOT contraindicated in patients with

opts.t: Local infection at the injection site
opts.why: Infection at the puncture site can inoculate deep tissue and is a contraindication.
An informed patient's refusal precludes an elective invasive regional procedure.

opts.t: Severe emphysema without a large apical bulla

opts.why: Significant uncorrected coagulopathy raises risk of bleeding/haematoma around deep neck structures.

questions.expl: Stellate ganglion block relative contraindications include infection, uncorrected coagulopathy and refusal. Severe pulmonary disease increases consequence of phrenic involvement or pneumothorax and requires caution, but is not necessarily an absolute contraindication.
questions.note: Source recalls 'severe emphysema' as the NOT contraindicated item; clinical assessment is still essential.

questions.stem: A four-year-old boy with a history of waddling gait, larger than normal calves and frequent falls receives a spontaneously breathing volatile-based anaesthetic with sevoflurane. One hour into the case he develops peaked T waves and then the end-tidal CO2 begins to rise. The most appropriate immediate treatment is to

opts.t: Give metoprolol for the peaked T waves
opts.why: Metoprolol does not stabilise hyperkalaemic myocardial membranes or treat the cause of peaked T waves.
Continued volatile exposure can aggravate dystrophinopathy-associated rhabdomyolysis.

opts.t: Give dantrolene alone and continue volatile
opts.why: Dantrolene is not sufficient for this Duchenne-type anaesthetic-induced hyperkalaemia, especially if volatile continues.

opts.t: Stop sevoflurane and give intravenous calcium for ECG evidence of hyperkalaemia

questions.expl: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is associated with anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis and potentially life-threatening hyperkalaemia. Stop triggers and stabilise the myocardium immediately with calcium while treating potassium and supporting resuscitation.
questions.note: Recalled answer distinguishes dystrophinopathy-associated rhabdomyolysis from classic malignant hyperthermia. Dantrolene may be considered if true MH cannot be excluded.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman requires a caesarean section delivery within 30 minutes for fetal distress. Her body mass index (BMI) is 26 kg/m2. She has multiple sclerosis with lesions in her brain and spinal cord and receives monthly injections of the disease-modifying drug ofatumumab. The most appropriate plan for her delivery is

opts.t: Avoid all neuraxial anaesthesia because of MS
opts.why: MS is not an absolute neuraxial contraindication; patient-specific assessment is required.

opts.t: Delay urgent delivery until neurology review
opts.why: Urgent delivery cannot wait for a routine neurology appointment without clear clinical indication.

opts.t: Spinal anaesthesia following individual risk assessment
General anaesthesia is obligatorily required in all MS
opts.why: General anaesthesia is not mandatory solely because of a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.

questions.expl: Multiple sclerosis is not itself a contraindication to neuraxial anaesthesia, and urgent caesarean section under spinal can be appropriate. Disease severity, neurological function and maternal condition guide choice.
questions.note: A 21.2-specific Brainscape key favours spinal. No evidence supports a blanket neuraxial prohibition.

questions.stem: You are examining the precordium of a patient in the preadmission clinic and hear a fourth heart sound at the apex. This finding is consistent with

opts.t: Severe mitral stenosis without atrial contraction
opts.why: Mitral stenosis may cause distinct murmurs, but absent atrial contraction cannot produce an atrial S₄.

opts.t: Systemic hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy
Physiological third heart sound of pregnancy
opts.why: The pregnancy-associated physiological sound is usually S₃ during early filling, not S₄.

opts.t: Isolated mitral regurgitation with a compliant ventricle
opts.why: Isolated regurgitation of a compliant ventricle is not the typical stiff-ventricle S₄ mechanism.

questions.expl: An S4 is caused by atrial contraction into a stiff, poorly compliant ventricle and is associated with hypertension, hypertrophy and ischaemia. A physiological S3 is a separate early-diastolic sound.

questions.stem: A patient with an acute subarachnoid haemorrhage arrives in the emergency department. Her Glasgow Coma Scale is 10 and she has no motor deficit. A CT brain shows diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage with no localised areas of blood > 1mm thick, and no intracerebral nor intraventricular blood. Her World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade of subarachnoid haemorrhage is

opts.why: WFNS grade II is reserved for GCS 13–14 without major motor deficit, not GCS 10.
Grade I denotes GCS 15 with no motor deficit.
Grade III requires GCS 13–14 with motor deficit, inconsistent with the described GCS.

opts.t: World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies grade IV

questions.expl: WFNS grades use GCS and focal deficit: GCS 7–12 is grade IV. The absence of motor deficit does not change this; CT blood distribution is a separate Fisher grade.

opts.why: Twelve months exceeds the historical minimum supervised training period.
One week is observational exposure, not the specified minimum training duration.
One month is below the three-month FTE minimum in period guidance.

questions.stem: In a patient with tetraplegia who develops autonomic dysreflexia, the expected haemodynamic response is

opts.why: Autonomic dysreflexia produces marked hypertension, not maintained normal pressure.
Reflex bradycardia can occur, but the pressure rise is hypertensive rather than hypotensive.
Tachycardia may occur occasionally, but hypotension is contrary to sympathetic vasoconstriction.

questions.expl: Autonomic dysreflexia after a high spinal cord lesion causes a sudden sympathetic vasoconstrictor surge below the lesion, with hypertension and often reflex bradycardia above the lesion.

questions.stem: The cardiac axis of this electrocardiogram is

opts.why: A positive lead I and negative inferior leads favour left, not right, deviation.
Northwest axis requires both lead I and aVF negative; that is not this representative tracing.

opts.t: Left axis deviation (illustrative ECG axis around −60 degrees)

opts.why: Inferior leads predominantly negative are not typical of a normal QRS axis here.

questions.stem: The most reliable clinical indicator of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment (OIVI) is decreased

opts.why: Heart rate is an insensitive and nonspecific early marker for opioid hypoventilation.
Respiratory count may miss shallow ventilation/airway obstruction and is not as reliable as increasing sedation.
Supplemental O₂ can mask hypoventilation, preserving SpO₂ until late.

questions.expl: Increasing sedation is often the most sensitive early clinical warning of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment. Pulse oximetry may remain normal on supplemental oxygen despite hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A patient presents for endovascular clot retrieval after experiencing a right hemisensory loss and right homonymous hemianopia. The vessel most likely occluded is the left

opts.why: PICA stroke produces cerebellar/lateral medullary signs rather than homonymous hemianopia.
AICA disease affects lateral pons/cerebellum, not occipital visual cortex.
ACA territory causes leg-predominant dysfunction, not the right homonymous visual deficit.

questions.expl: A left PCA infarct can involve both occipital cortex (right homonymous hemianopia) and thalamus (right hemisensory deficit). Cerebellar arteries do not explain the cortical visual deficit.

questions.stem: The function of the bottle labelled 'D' in the diagram below is to protect against the consequences of

opts.t: Pleural-fluid drainage exceeding the collection bottle
opts.why: Collection bottle overflow is managed by drainage capacity and does not explain the relief chamber's function.
Excessive negative suction is limited by the suction-regulating water column, a different bottle.
Chest tube depth is a patient-placement issue, not corrected by adding a pressure-relief chamber.

questions.expl: In a four-bottle underwater-seal drainage system, the fourth atmospheric pressure-relief chamber prevents air entry into pleural space or pneumothorax if wall suction abruptly fails. The suction-regulating bottle controls excessive suction instead.
questions.note: Four-bottle reconstruction matches the reported bottle-D function, not the simpler three-bottle device.

questions.stem: A trainee becomes aware that a patient they have just anaesthetised for emergency surgery is breastfeeding and seeks your advice regarding recommencement of breast feeding. You advise that breast feeding is contraindicated because during the admission today the patient received

opts.why: Sevoflurane is rapidly eliminated and normal breast-feeding can resume once recovered.
Propofol has low breast-milk transfer after a single anaesthetic and does not generally require interruption.

opts.t: Fentanyl used as a single perioperative dose
opts.why: A single perioperative fentanyl dose is compatible with usual resumption once the mother is alert; avoid excessive ongoing exposure.

questions.expl: Codeine metabolism to morphine varies with CYP2D6 genotype and can expose breastfeeding infants to opioid toxicity. Routine breast-feeding may generally resume after many anaesthetic agents when the mother is awake and alert.
questions.note: 2021 recall suggests codeine; check current national drug advice for lactation and individual use.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing robotic prostatectomy with volume-controlled ventilation has the following ventilatory measurements: (Ventilator parameters given) The static compliance is

opts.why: 25 mL/cmH₂O follows an incorrect pressure subtraction; include auto-PEEP to get denominator 20.
38 mL/cmH₂O wrongly incorporates resistance/peak pressure or an incorrect denominator.
20 mL/cmH₂O does not equal 600 mL divided by the 20-cmH₂O driving pressure.

questions.expl: Static compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus total PEEP: 600/(32 − [8+4]) = 30 mL/cmH₂O. Peak pressure includes flow resistance and is not used.
questions.note: The omitted original ventilator results were recovered from a matching Anki recall; reconstructed table provided.

questions.stem: When performing cannulation of the median cubital vein the structure that is LEAST likely to be inadvertently punctured or damaged is the

opts.why: A deep needle can injure the brachial artery near the antecubital fossa.
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve courses superficially near the cubital region and can be injured.
The median nerve is relatively close to the brachial artery deep in the fossa.

questions.expl: Median cubital vein venepuncture can injure nearby superficial sensory branches and, if deep, the brachial artery or median nerve; the ulnar nerve at the wrist is anatomically remote from the antecubital fossa.
questions.note: Actual answer options absent. This is an intentionally unambiguous practice exception rather than an authenticated answer to the original options.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) physical staus classification 1 patient develops seizures five minutes after receiving a brachial plexus block with ropivacaine. Of the following, the most suitable initial intravenous treatment is

opts.t: Intravenous calcium gluconate as seizure treatment
opts.why: Calcium does not terminate LAST seizures and does not treat sodium-channel toxicity itself.

opts.t: Intravenous phenytoin as immediate first-line treatment
opts.why: Phenytoin is not preferred first-line seizure treatment in LAST.

opts.t: A large propofol bolus as sole therapy
opts.why: A large propofol bolus risks haemodynamic collapse and is inappropriate as sole therapy.

questions.expl: Stop local anaesthetic injection, summon help and give benzodiazepine for LAST-associated seizures, with lipid emulsion available promptly. Large propofol doses can worsen cardiovascular collapse; calcium and phenytoin are not preferred immediate anticonvulsants.

questions.stem: Complications of hyperbaric oxygen therapy include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Middle-ear pressure injury is a frequent HBOT complication.

opts.t: Carboxyhaemoglobin of 10% alone in an asymptomatic person

opts.why: Reversible lens changes/myopia occur with repeated high-pressure oxygen exposure.
Hyperoxic CNS toxicity can cause tonic-clonic seizures during HBOT.

questions.expl: Ear barotrauma, visual changes and oxygen-toxicity seizures are recognised complications of hyperbaric oxygen therapy. A COHb of 10% is an indication-related finding, not a complication of the therapy.
questions.note: The original 'EXCEPT' options were unavailable; reconstructed distractors test indication versus complication.

questions.stem: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a statistical test to determine

opts.t: A difference between means across three or more groups
Correlation between two continuous variables only
opts.why: Correlation uses Pearson/Spearman-type methods to measure association rather than ANOVA mean differences.
Two categorical proportions are compared by tests such as chi-square or proportion tests.
Agreement between raters requires kappa, ICC or Bland–Altman methods as appropriate.

questions.expl: Analysis of variance tests equality of group mean values, with the F statistic comparing within- and between-group variability. It does not principally measure correlation, proportion differences or observer agreement.

questions.stem: The oral morphine equivalent of tapentadol 50 mg (immediate release) is

opts.why: Fifty mg morphine would imply near 1:1 equivalence and overestimate tapentadol potency.
150 mg morphine would grossly overestimate the equianalgesic effect of 50 mg tapentadol.
One mg morphine grossly underestimates the analgesic effect of 50 mg tapentadol.

questions.expl: Common equianalgesic conversion tables approximate oral tapentadol 50 mg to oral morphine 15–20 mg; equivalence is imperfect because of different mechanisms and must not be used to switch strong opioids without safety margins.
questions.note: Published conversion ratios vary. This uses the original recalled 15 mg approximation.

questions.stem: Allergic cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is mediated by the

opts.t: Cross-reactivity of the entire beta-lactam nucleus in every patient
opts.why: The beta-lactam nucleus alone does not produce universal cross-reactivity across agents.

opts.t: Shared inhibition of bacterial folate synthesis
opts.why: Cephalosporins act on bacterial cell wall PBPs, not folate metabolism.
Sharing renal excretion is pharmacokinetic and unrelated to IgE antigen recognition.

questions.expl: Cephalosporin–penicillin allergy cross-reactivity is primarily associated with similar side-chain determinants, particularly R₁. The four-membered beta-lactam ring is not sufficient to predict uniform cross-reactivity.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man suffers a burn involving 30% of his total body surface area. A cardiovascular physiological change expected within the first twenty-four hours is

opts.why: Initial burn shock causes low organ perfusion, not increased hepatic flow.
Bradycardia without hypotension is not the characteristic high-catecholamine haemodynamic response.

opts.t: Reduced cardiac output and reduced hepatic/renal perfusion early after the burn
Immediate sustained high-output circulation without resuscitation
opts.why: High-output hypermetabolism is a later phase, not immediate sustained physiology without resuscitation.

questions.expl: The initial 24–48 hours after major burns can involve hypovolaemia, capillary leak and a low-output shock phase. The later hypermetabolic high-output response is distinct.

questions.stem: Of the following, the incidence of venous air embolism is considered highest for (list of surgical procedures given)

opts.why: Supine laparoscopy has less persistent venous-to-heart negative pressure gradient than sitting intracranial venous exposure.

opts.t: Sitting neurosurgery with the operative field above the heart

opts.why: Cataract surgery does not usually expose large noncollapsible venous channels above right atrial level.

opts.t: Routine lower-limb orthopaedics in the supine position
opts.why: Routine supine lower-limb surgery carries lower air-entrainment pressure gradient.

questions.expl: An open venous circulation above right atrial level, as during sitting neurosurgery, creates a pressure gradient that favours air entrainment and a high incidence of venous air embolism.
questions.note: Actual comparison procedures were not provided; this is a reconstructed high-incidence example.

questions.stem: Intraoperative cell salvage is contraindicated in

opts.why: Some Jehovah's Witness patients permit continuous-circuit cell salvage after individual discussion.

opts.t: Contamination with a substance that lyses red cells, such as hydrogen peroxide

opts.why: Obstetric salvage can be performed under appropriate washing/filtration protocols.
Cancer surgery is not a universal absolute prohibition; selection and leukocyte filters may be appropriate.

questions.expl: Cell salvage should not be used where aspirated blood is chemically incompatible with cells or substantially contaminated with unsuitable substances. Malignancy and obstetric use may be feasible under protocols; some Jehovah's Witness patients accept continuous-circuit salvage.
questions.note: Strong or absolute contraindications vary by equipment, field contamination and local protocol.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman who is spontaneously breathing through a tracheostomy tube with an inner cannula becomes acutely breathless. Despite application of high flow oxygen, her respiratory rate is 40 breaths per minute and her SpO2 is 82%. The next most appropriate step in her airway management is to

opts.t: Remove the whole mature tracheostomy before checking patency
opts.why: Removing a whole tracheostomy prematurely may be hazardous; inspect the removable inner cannula first.

opts.t: Remove and inspect the inner cannula immediately
Increase the oxygen flow without checking the tube
opts.why: Oxygen alone cannot overcome complete inner-cannula obstruction.
Oral feeding is irrelevant and dangerous during an acute airway emergency.

questions.expl: Acute distress in a tracheostomy with inner cannula may reflect mucus plugging. Remove the inner cannula, assess airflow and suction as indicated while escalating according to the national tracheostomy emergency algorithm.

questions.stem: The anion which contributes the most to the anion gap is

opts.t: Albumin, as the predominant unmeasured physiological anion

opts.why: Chloride is included explicitly as a measured anion and subtracted in the standard equation.
Bicarbonate is another measured subtracted anion, not an unmeasured component.
Sodium is the principal measured cation in the equation, not the relevant unmeasured anion.

questions.expl: In the common equation AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃), chloride and bicarbonate are measured subtracted anions; albumin is the largest routinely unmeasured anion contributing to a normal anion gap.

questions.stem: Of the following drugs, the least likely to cause pulmonary vasodilation when used at low doses in patients with chronic pulmonary hypertension is

opts.why: Epoprostenol is a prostacyclin vasodilator that reduces PVR, particularly by inhalation.

opts.t: Phenylephrine at a systemic vasopressor dose

opts.why: Sildenafil blocks PDE5 to increase cGMP and relax pulmonary vascular smooth muscle.
Inhaled NO selectively dilates ventilated pulmonary vasculature.

questions.expl: Phenylephrine primarily causes systemic alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and may increase pulmonary vascular resistance, unlike NO, prostacyclin and PDE5 inhibitors that reduce pulmonary resistance.
questions.note: The original list is unavailable. This is a reconstructed comparison of pulmonary-selective vasodilators versus a vasoconstrictor.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman is administered two doses of aprepitant for postoperative nausea and vomiting after a sleeve gastrectomy. She normally takes the oral contraceptive pill. You should advise her to use alternative contraception for the next

opts.t: One month after the final aprepitant dose

opts.why: Three days is shorter than the one-month backup contraception duration in aprepitant labelling.
Forty-eight hours does not cover the enzyme-mediated reduction in contraceptive efficacy.
Twenty-four hours is much shorter than the required precaution following the final dose.

questions.expl: Aprepitant may decrease effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives through enzyme effects. Product information recommends a non-hormonal backup during treatment and for one month after the final dose.

questions.stem: A patient who usually takes oral morphine 50 mg bd develops a bowel obstruction and experiences withdrawal symptoms. They may be described as having

opts.why: Tolerance means less effect from a given opioid dose; it does not itself explain withdrawal.
An allergy would cause immune-type adverse symptoms, not characteristic opioid withdrawal after cessation.
Expected physiological dependence from prescribed morphine does not prove a compulsive substance-use disorder.

questions.expl: Withdrawal symptoms on abrupt cessation of regular morphine demonstrate physiological physical dependence, which can occur without addiction. Tolerance is reduced response to a fixed dose rather than the withdrawal phenomenon itself.
questions.note: The earlier Anki recall labelled tolerance, but physical dependence is the more precise explanation for withdrawal.

questions.stem: The image below on the left shows a normal central venous pressure (CVP) trace. The CVP trace in the image below on the right is most consistent with

opts.t: Tricuspid regurgitation with giant systolic v waves

opts.why: Normal CVP waveforms have a and v waves without giant fused systolic c-v excursions.
Simple hypovolaemia lowers mean pressure but does not create prominent systolic v waves.

opts.t: Isolated pulmonary stenosis with unchanged atrial waveform
opts.why: Pulmonary stenosis alters RV outflow and does not characteristically produce the same tricuspid regurgitant atrial waveform.

questions.expl: Tricuspid regurgitation produces prominent systolic right-atrial c-v waves as RV systolic pressure is transmitted backward. The recalled trace shows this characteristic feature.
questions.note: A recalled explanatory CVP trace is included; the original ANZCA tracing is unavailable.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is brought into the Emergency Department four hours after an accidental chemical exposure during crop spraying. His clinical signs include bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea, coughing, miosis and weakness. A drug which is NOT recommended during his resuscitation and treatment is

opts.why: Atropine reverses muscarinic bradycardia/bronchorrhoea and is part of poisoning management.
Oxygenation/ventilation are essential supportive treatment, not a drug uniquely prohibited here.
Pralidoxime can reactivate inhibited acetylcholinesterase if given appropriately.

questions.expl: Organophosphate toxicity inhibits acetylcholinesterase and often plasma cholinesterase, so suxamethonium can produce profoundly prolonged paralysis. Atropine and oximes are mainstays in appropriate poisoning management.

questions.stem: A new volatile agent is developed. The property it shares with sevoflurane that will enable it to be used in a sevoflurane vapouriser and deliver an accurate concentration is its

opts.why: Oil–gas partition affects agent solubility in lipid but not calibrated vapouriser output.

opts.t: Saturated vapour pressure at the operating temperature

opts.why: Blood–gas partition determines blood uptake/induction kinetics, not saturated vapour pressure.
MAC describes clinical potency rather than physical vapouriser calibration.

questions.expl: A variable-bypass, agent-calibrated vaporiser depends strongly on the volatile agent's saturated vapour pressure to deliver accurate calibrated concentrations. Blood/gas solubility influences uptake, not machine output calibration.

questions.stem: When performing a brachial plexus block at the level of the axilla, the structure indicated by the arrow is the

opts.why: The pleural dome is a thoracic/neck structure, not the landmark for axillary blockade.
Femoral artery lies in the groin and cannot be the vessel in the axillary ultrasound.

opts.t: The brachial artery near the elbow
opts.why: The brachial artery is distal as the axillary vessel continues down the arm; the depicted level is axillary.

questions.expl: Ultrasound-guided axillary brachial plexus blocks orient median, ulnar, radial and musculocutaneous nerves around the axillary artery. The reconstructed image labels this central landmark.
questions.note: The original arrow was not reproduced; representative image shows the central axillary artery rather than proving the original arrow location.

questions.stem: The diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is likely to be decreased with

opts.why: Uncomplicated asthma often has normal or increased DLCO rather than reduced diffusion.

opts.t: Simple obesity without intrinsic lung disease
opts.why: Isolated obesity may have preserved/increased diffusing capacity without parenchymal disease.

opts.t: Interstitial lung disease such as sarcoidosis

opts.why: Alveolar haemorrhage transiently raises DLCO because intra-alveolar haemoglobin binds CO.

questions.expl: DLCO falls with interstitial fibrosis, emphysema, anaemia and pulmonary vascular disease. It may be preserved or high in asthma and alveolar haemorrhage; isolated obesity does not typically reduce it.

questions.stem: The use of erythropoietin before major surgery results in

opts.t: No effect on haemoglobin or transfusion
opts.why: Erythropoietin generally raises haemoglobin and may reduce transfusion in appropriately selected patients.
Mortality reduction has not been reliably shown and cannot be assumed from increased red-cell mass.
Transfusions usually decrease, not increase, when preoperative erythropoiesis is effective.

opts.t: Reduced allogeneic transfusion requirements, with higher perioperative haemoglobin

questions.expl: Perioperative erythropoietin generally decreases transfusion exposure in selected surgical populations when combined with iron, though thrombosis risk, cost and patient selection still matter. Mortality benefit is not established.

questions.stem: Predictors of successful awake extubation after volatile anaesthesia in infants include

opts.why: Apnoea means inadequate spontaneous breathing and is unsafe for awake extubation.

opts.t: Purposeful leg extension or purposeful movement during emergence

opts.why: Unresponsiveness indicates that the infant has not regained protective arousal.
Absent protective reflexes increase risk of aspiration or airway obstruction.

questions.expl: Purposeful movement, adequate ventilation and return of protective reflexes are reassuring signs during awake infant extubation; age, clinical condition and the specific assessment of eye opening or leg extension matter.
questions.note: Recalled studies used leg extension as a predictor; this alone is not an extubation checklist.

questions.stem: The maximum warm ischaemia time acceptable for procuring the kidney following donation after circulatory death (DCD) is

opts.why: Five minutes is substantially below many kidney DCD functional warm-ischaemia limits.
Six hours is far beyond usual accepted kidney warm-ischaemia limits.
Ten minutes is too restrictive for the described kidney donation threshold.

opts.t: Approximately 60 minutes of warm ischaemia for a kidney

questions.expl: Organ-specific limits vary; among commonly recalled thresholds kidneys may tolerate approximately 60 min warm ischaemia in controlled donation after circulatory death, longer than heart or liver. Actual transplant programmes use functional warm-ischaemia definitions.
questions.note: The exact acceptance threshold is programme- and organ-condition-specific; 60 minutes is a recalled reference value.

questions.stem: The risk of postoperative respiratory failure in myasthenia gravis is increased by the administration of

opts.why: Cefazolin is a beta-lactam without the characteristic strong aminoglycoside neuromuscular blockade.
Teicoplanin is not a usual cause of NMJ transmission failure in myasthenia.
Flucloxacillin does not have the classic aminoglycoside presynaptic/post-synaptic weakness effect.

questions.expl: Aminoglycosides impair neuromuscular transmission and can worsen myasthenia gravis, increasing risk of ventilatory failure. The other antibiotics are not classic strong neuromuscular transmission blockers in routine dosing.

questions.stem: A patient with known type 3 von Willebrand disease presents with persistent epistaxis. First- line medical therapy should include

opts.why: DDAVP cannot release significant VWF in type 3 disease because stores are nearly absent.
Vitamin K treats deficiency of vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors, not absent VWF.
Warfarin further impairs haemostasis and is inappropriate for active epistaxis.

opts.t: Tranexamic acid as an adjunct, with urgent vWF-containing factor replacement when needed

questions.expl: Type 3 von Willebrand disease has virtually absent vWF, so desmopressin is ineffective. Antifibrinolytics help mucosal bleeding, but significant or persistent bleeding may require vWF/FVIII concentrate and specialist guidance.
questions.note: The Anki recall keyed TXA as first-line adjunct; do not treat TXA as sufficient for severe type 3 vWD bleeding.

questions.stem: ANZCA fasting guidelines classify all of the following as clear fluids EXCEPT

opts.why: Plain cordial without particulate matter meets traditional clear-fluid criteria.
Pulp-free apple juice is generally an accepted clear fluid.
Water is the canonical fasting-guideline clear fluid.

questions.expl: Milk-containing beverages are not classified as clear liquids under the traditional fasting definition. Water, pulp-free juice and clear cordial are transparent, non-particulate clear fluids.
questions.note: Some newer policies permit selected milk-containing drinks in specified quantities; examine the period-specific guideline and local policy.

questions.stem: A patient has return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) but remains unresponsive after cardiac arrest. ANZCOR Guidelines recommend all the following measures EXCEPT

opts.t: Glucose monitoring and preventing severe hypo-/hyperglycaemia
opts.why: Glucose management prevents metabolic cerebral injury and is recommended after ROSC.
Preventing hypoxaemia and hypotension is central to post-arrest care.

opts.t: Targeted temperature control and fever prevention
opts.why: Temperature control/fever prevention are recommended components of post-ROSC care.

opts.t: Routine deliberate hyperoxia with PaO₂ far above physiological range

questions.expl: After ROSC, care aims to avoid hypoxaemia, hyperoxia, hypotension and temperature extremes, while treating seizures and maintaining perfusion. Intentionally sustained severe hyperoxaemia is not recommended.
questions.note: The recalled original option set is incomplete. Current post-arrest temperature wording has evolved since 2021.

questions.stem: Your patient has been administered 50 mL of oral 5–aminolevulinic acid hydrochloride (Gliolan) three hours prior to her scheduled craniotomy for resection of a glioblastoma. Care should be taken perioperatively to avoid the adverse effect of

opts.why: Ductal closure is not a recognised systemic effect of ALA used for glioma fluorescence.
ALA is not an established triggering agent for malignant hyperthermia.

opts.t: Immediate haemolysis from all red-cell transfusions
opts.why: ALA does not universally haemolyse transfused erythrocytes; photosensitivity is the expected precaution.

questions.expl: Oral 5-aminolevulinic acid causes selective protoporphyrin IX accumulation and temporary photosensitivity; avoid high-intensity light exposure after dosing. Hypotension and liver-enzyme disturbances are also possible.

questions.stem: The most common cause of mortality in children with diabetic ketoacidosis is

opts.why: Mild phosphate reduction rarely explains the principal fatal complication of paediatric DKA.
Appendicitis may mimic abdominal pain but is not the characteristic cause of paediatric DKA death.
Cholesterol elevation is unrelated to acute cerebral injury during DKA management.

questions.expl: Cerebral injury is a leading cause of DKA-related morbidity and mortality in children. The presentation and management require careful fluid/electrolyte monitoring and rapid recognition of neurological deterioration.

questions.stem: An electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormality which is NOT usually associated with severe anorexia nervosa is

opts.why: QT prolongation can accompany malnutrition, medication use and electrolyte deficits.
Sinus bradycardia is a classic physiological finding in severe restrictive eating disorders.
Low QRS voltage can reflect reduced body mass and associated physiological changes.

opts.t: Pathological Q waves as a characteristic isolated effect of starvation

questions.expl: Severe anorexia nervosa commonly causes sinus bradycardia, QT issues and low voltage, often related to malnutrition and electrolyte disturbances. Pathological Q waves suggest infarction or other pathology rather than anorexia alone.
questions.note: Original ECG options unavailable; reconstructed exception.

questions.stem: You have been asked to provide general anaesthesia for a complex thoracic endovascular aortic aneurysm repair. After the placement of a lumbar drain the recommended safe time before the administration of intravenous heparin is

opts.t: Twenty-four hours for every uncomplicated single placement
opts.why: Twenty-four hours is longer than the advised minimum after uncomplicated neuraxial puncture.

opts.t: At least one hour between lumbar puncture/drain placement and systemic heparinisation

opts.why: Immediate systemic heparin raises neuraxial bleeding risk immediately after the puncture.
Five minutes does not allow the recommended interval before anticoagulation.

questions.expl: Regional anaesthesia/neuraxial anticoagulation guidance generally recommends allowing at least an hour between uncomplicated neuraxial needle placement and systemic IV heparin. Longer delays may be appropriate after traumatic puncture.
questions.note: Follow local vascular/spinal-drain anticoagulation protocols; not a universally safe interval for traumatic insertion.

questions.stem: The image below shows results from non inferiority trials. The trial labelled 'M' is best described as

opts.t: An equivalence finding without a superiority test
opts.why: Equivalence requires two-sided prespecified margins; a favourable CI beyond the superiority line supports more than equivalence alone.

opts.t: A trial clearly inferior to control
opts.why: An inferior trial has confidence bounds unfavourable to treatment rather than wholly on the beneficial side.

opts.t: Non-inferiority with evidence of superiority in the illustrated result

opts.why: Failure of non-inferiority occurs when the CI crosses the non-inferiority margin, not when fully on the beneficial side.

questions.expl: If a trial's confidence interval lies entirely on the favourable side of both the non-inferiority margin and the no-difference line, it may demonstrate both non-inferiority and superiority. A representative graph showing these margins is supplied.
questions.note: The reported original panel M was not released; reconstructed figure teaches the recalled classification only.

questions.stem: Painless post-operative visual loss with preserved pupillary reflexes is most likely due to

opts.why: Corneal abrasion causes pain/photophobia, not isolated painless cortical-type visual loss.
Optic-nerve ischaemia usually produces an afferent pupillary abnormality in unilateral/asymmetric cases.
Central retinal artery occlusion typically causes a marked afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye.

questions.expl: Preserved pupillary light reflexes with painless bilateral visual loss imply a lesion posterior to the pretectal pathway, such as occipital cortex. Retinal and optic-nerve damage typically alter afferent pupillary responses, while abrasion is painful.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man is admitted with a stroke and undergoes cerebral angiography. The artery marked with an arrow on the angiogram below is the

opts.why: AICA is a small lateral brainstem/cerebellar vessel, not the lateral Sylvian branch shown.
PCA arises near basilar apex and supplies posterior cerebral cortex, rather than the MCA territory shown.
Basilar is a midline vertebrobasilar trunk, not a lateral internal-carotid branch.

questions.expl: An MCA branch can be recognised on a representative cerebral angiogram as a lateral extension from the internal carotid bifurcation supplying the Sylvian territory. Distinguish from ACA projecting medially and PCA from basilar apex.

questions.stem: The oculocardiac reflex results in

opts.t: Predictable tachycardia with no blood-pressure change
opts.why: Oculocardiac stimulation is vagally mediated and ordinarily slows, not accelerates, the heart.
Hypothermia is not the direct output of the trigemino-vagal reflex.
Bronchodilatation is unrelated to the extraocular traction reflex.

opts.t: Reflex bradycardia, usually greater than a 20% heart-rate fall

questions.expl: Traction on an extraocular muscle stimulates trigeminal afferents and vagal efferents, producing bradycardia, dysrhythmia or asystole. Release traction and treat physiologically significant bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of restless leg syndrome is agitated in the post-anaesthesia care unit. After excluding other causes, the best treatment of the agitation in this patient is

opts.why: Droperidol blocks D₂ receptors and can worsen restless-leg symptoms.

opts.t: Midazolam after assessment and exclusion of other agitation causes

opts.why: Haloperidol's dopamine antagonism may exacerbate RLS and akathisia.
Metoclopramide also blocks dopamine and can worsen restlessness.

questions.expl: Restless legs can be exacerbated by dopamine-antagonist agents; benzodiazepine may settle acute postoperative distress once hypoxia, pain and other causes are excluded. Chronic RLS treatment is different.
questions.note: Reconstructed recall; medication choice should be individualised.

questions.stem: With regard to the risk of postoperative surgical-site infection, 8 mg dexamethasone administered intraoperatively has

opts.why: PADDI did not show a reliable doubling of infection following a single 8-mg dose.

opts.t: An absolute contraindication in all diabetics
opts.why: Diabetes warrants glucose monitoring, not a blanket contraindication to one intraoperative dose.

opts.t: No clinically important increase in surgical-site infection at a single 8 mg dose
A proven increase in deep wound infections in all populations
opts.why: A consistent increase in deep wound infection in all patients was not demonstrated.

questions.expl: The large PADDI trial found single-dose intraoperative dexamethasone was non-inferior to placebo for surgical-site infection. Glucose can rise transiently, so monitor in at-risk patients.

questions.stem: Intraoperative lung protective ventilation strategies include all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Tailored PEEP can limit atelectrauma and is part of lung-protective ventilation.

opts.t: An I:E ratio of 1:3 as a mandatory universal lung-protective setting

opts.why: Modest predicted-body-weight tidal volumes limit volutrauma.
Avoiding excessive plateau/driving pressures limits pressure-related lung injury.

questions.expl: Lung-protective ventilation emphasises small tidal volumes, pressure limitation and appropriate PEEP. There is no universal protective I:E of 1:3; longer expiration may be chosen for obstruction, not all patients.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman is dyspnoeic after a total hip replacement. A lung ultrasound is performed in the post-anaesthesia care unit, with a still image shown below. The likely cause of the dyspnoea is

opts.t: Vertical B-line artefacts arising at the pleura

opts.why: A lung point is the boundary of sliding/no sliding, favouring pneumothorax over interstitial B-lines.
A-lines are horizontal repetitive pleural echoes, not deep vertical artefacts.
An effusion is an anechoic dependent fluid collection, not bright reverberation streaks.

questions.expl: B-lines are bright vertical artefacts extending from the pleural line to the bottom of the screen and can indicate interstitial syndrome. A-lines are horizontal; lung point supports pneumothorax, not interstitial artefacts.

questions.stem: Local anaesthetic-induced myotoxicity is most likely to be associated with

opts.t: Continuous high-concentration bupivacaine local anaesthetic exposure

opts.why: Normal saline does not have the myotoxic local-anaesthetic pharmacology described.
A small saline flush has no sustained tissue exposure to myotoxic bupivacaine.
Oxygen treatment does not cause direct local anaesthetic muscle toxicity.

questions.expl: Local anaesthetic myotoxicity is concentration- and exposure-dependent and is particularly concerning with continuous catheter infusions or intramuscular injection. Bupivacaine can produce muscle necrosis and regeneration over time.

questions.stem: The abnormality shown in this image is LEAST likely to be caused by an injury to the

opts.why: Spinal accessory palsy affects trapezius and can give abnormal scapular winging.

opts.t: Suprascapular nerve injury as the least typical cause of prominent medial scapular winging

opts.why: Long thoracic nerve damage disables serratus anterior, producing classic medial winging.
Dorsal scapular injury weakens rhomboids and can disturb scapular stabilisation.

questions.expl: Classical medial scapular winging follows serratus anterior weakness from long thoracic injury. Trapezius and rhomboid dysfunction can also alter scapular motion; suprascapular nerve injury mainly weakens supraspinatus/infraspinatus.

questions.stem: Postdural puncture headache in obstetric anaesthesia is associated with a greater likelihood of all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Subdural collections can follow intracranial hypotension and bridging-vein traction.
Cerebral venous thrombosis is a recognised complication/association of intracranial hypotension.

opts.t: Encephalitis as the least characteristic association

opts.why: Seizure and other neurological deficits may occur with intracranial complications after CSF leak.

questions.expl: Postdural-puncture headache and intracranial hypotension are associated with venous thrombosis and subdural collections. Encephalitis is not a characteristic direct complication of CSF leak.
questions.note: Older recall incorrectly suggested stroke as the exception, but postpartum stroke is reported in association with PDPH.

questions.stem: The most common type of perioperative stroke is

opts.why: Haemorrhagic stroke occurs but accounts for a smaller proportion than perioperative ischaemia.
Cerebral abscess is infectious rather than a usual perioperative stroke mechanism.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is a subset of bleeding cerebrovascular events, not the most common.

questions.expl: Perioperative strokes are predominantly ischaemic, with embolic or thrombotic mechanisms; haemorrhage is a smaller subset.

questions.stem: Hepcidin production is inhibited in response to

opts.why: Iron overload stimulates hepcidin to limit further iron uptake.
Excess stored iron increases, rather than suppresses, hepcidin.
IL-6 during inflammation upregulates hepcidin and sequesters circulating iron.

questions.expl: Hepcidin falls when erythropoiesis needs iron and with iron deficiency or hypoxia, promoting ferroportin activity and absorption. It rises with inflammation and iron excess.

questions.stem: The most common cause of cor pulmonale is

opts.why: Coarctation creates systemic afterload rather than primary chronic lung-mediated right-heart failure.
A left atrial myxoma is an intracardiac lesion, not the usual pulmonary cause of cor pulmonale.
Mitral stenosis produces postcapillary pulmonary hypertension from left-heart disease, excluded from classic cor pulmonale.

opts.t: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic hypoxic lung disease

questions.expl: Cor pulmonale is right-ventricular dysfunction caused by pulmonary disease or pulmonary hypertension, most commonly chronic lung disease including COPD. Left-heart valvular disease causes secondary pulmonary hypertension but is excluded from the classical cor pulmonale definition.

questions.stem: A risk factor which increases the likelihood of developing local anaesthetic systemic toxicity is

opts.why: High albumin usually increases protein binding and lowers free drug fraction rather than heightening LAST risk.
Dilution may reduce concentration but does not inherently increase toxicity.
Normal pregnancy can change local anaesthetic sensitivity, but the recalled distinctive metabolic risk was carnitine deficiency.

questions.expl: Carnitine deficiency can impair cardiac fatty-acid metabolism and increases susceptibility to local anaesthetic toxicity, particularly cardiotoxicity. Intrinsic factors such as low cardiac reserve, liver disease and acidosis also matter.

questions.stem: The medical laser LEAST likely to cause eye injury is

opts.why: Green light is absorbed by retinal pigments and can cause retinal injury.
Nd:YAG near-infrared light penetrates ocular media and can damage posterior structures.

opts.t: Carbon dioxide laser (10,600 nm) as least likely to damage the retina

opts.why: Argon visible light can be focused onto retina and is hazardous without eye protection.

questions.expl: CO₂ radiation is absorbed largely at the ocular surface and threatens the cornea rather than reaching the retina. Visible and near-infrared lasers can penetrate to and injure retinal tissues. None are safe without protective eyewear.
questions.note: The word 'eye injury' is broad: CO₂ can still cause serious corneal injury; this is the recalled retina-centric exam distinction.

questions.stem: The main advantage of using noradrenaline (norepinephrine) over phenylephrine for the prevention of hypotension as a result of spinal anaesthesia for elective caesarean section is

opts.t: Direct improvement in fetal heart rate independent of blood pressure
opts.why: Preserving maternal HR/CO is the main observed advantage, not a direct fetal HR effect independent of pressure.
Increased nausea is not an advantage and is not the defining norepinephrine effect.
Noradrenaline is used to prevent/treat hypotension, not because it causes more of it.

questions.expl: Noradrenaline retains modest beta activity, tending to preserve maternal heart rate and cardiac output compared with pure alpha agonist phenylephrine during spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section.

questions.stem: Of the following, the LEAST likely cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis is

opts.why: Lactate accumulation introduces unmeasured anions and raises the anion gap.
Methanol generates formate, producing marked high-gap acidosis.
Ketoacids are unmeasured organic anions and cause high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.expl: Loss of bicarbonate from diarrhoea produces a predominantly normal-anion-gap hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Ketoacids, lactate and toxic alcohol metabolites produce high unmeasured anions and high anion gap.

questions.stem: The most common complication of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in adults is

opts.why: Airway injury is not the most common ECMO circuit-related complication.
Stroke is serious but less frequent than bleeding in typical ECMO series.
Oxygenator failure can occur but is not usually the most frequent adverse event.

questions.expl: Bleeding is among the most common complications directly attributable to ECMO, due to anticoagulation, cannulation and acquired haemostatic defects. AKI and infection are common in critically ill ECMO populations, but have multifactorial causes.

questions.stem: The power board on the back of the anaesthesia machine has caught fire during an elective case. This should be extinguished with

opts.t: Foam extinguisher sprayed over energised equipment
opts.why: Foam over energised equipment can introduce contamination and is unsuitable for that electrical fire class.

opts.t: Water poured over the power supply
opts.why: Water conducts electricity and is unsafe when applied to energised power supplies.
Alcohol spray is flammable and can enlarge, not extinguish, the fire.

questions.expl: A CO₂ extinguisher is appropriate for energised electrical equipment in the operating theatre, alongside isolating the supply when safe. Water and some agents add electrical or contamination hazards.

questions.stem: The most common presenting rhythm associated with maternal cardiac arrest is

opts.why: Monomorphic VT is less common as the initial rhythm than a nonshockable PEA arrest in maternal registries.
A pulsed SVT is not an arrest rhythm.
VF occurs but is not the most frequently reported maternal arrest rhythm.

questions.expl: Observational maternal cardiac-arrest registries report PEA as the most frequent presenting rhythm; causes include haemorrhage, embolism and severe hypoxia.

questions.stem: The number of segments in the lower lobe of the left lung is

opts.why: Eight exceeds the usual four described left lower-lobe segments.
Two omits the superior and basal bronchopulmonary segments.
Twelve far exceeds the segment count within a single lung lobe.

questions.expl: The left lower lobe is commonly described as having four bronchopulmonary segments: superior, anteromedial basal, lateral basal and posterior basal. Segmental nomenclature can separate anterior and medial components in variants.

questions.stem: Cardiovascular effects of hyperthyroidism include

opts.why: Thyroid excess usually increases cardiac output and contractility.
Peripheral vasodilatation tends to lower, not raise, diastolic arterial pressure.

opts.t: Bradycardia due to reduced sympathetic responsiveness
opts.why: Resting tachycardia and increased adrenergic responsiveness are typical, not bradycardia.

opts.t: Reduced systemic vascular resistance and widened pulse pressure

questions.expl: Hyperthyroidism causes increased heart rate and contractility, higher cardiac output, and peripheral vasodilatation with reduced SVR and often lower diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: The coagulopathy that can result from intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is due to

opts.why: Cholestasis does not characteristically generate acquired factor-VIII autoantibodies.
Platelet immune destruction is a different mechanism from impaired vitamin absorption.

opts.t: Vitamin K malabsorption with deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

opts.why: Increased antithrombin synthesis would not explain loss of vitamin-K-dependent clotting activity.

questions.expl: Bile is needed for fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Cholestasis can impair vitamin K uptake and reduce functional factors II, VII, IX and X, causing a coagulopathy.

questions.stem: A man who had successful treatment of a germ cell tumour ten years ago presents for laparoscopic appendectomy. Your intraoperative management should consider

opts.why: Avoiding all IV fluid risks hypoperfusion; the principle is conservative judicious fluid rather than absolute abstention.

opts.t: Avoid unnecessary high inspired oxygen concentrations after prior bleomycin exposure
Administer routine high-dose oxygen irrespective of need
opts.why: Routine excess oxygen can aggravate toxicity risk and should be titrated to oxygenation needs.

opts.t: Assume bleomycin exposure always causes malignant hyperthermia
opts.why: Bleomycin is not a malignant-hyperthermia trigger; the concern is lung injury and oxygen exposure.

questions.expl: Bleomycin may produce pulmonary toxicity, and high FiO₂ can exacerbate injury in susceptible patients. Modern practice avoids unnecessary hyperoxia while maintaining adequate oxygenation; restrictive fluids may also be considered.
questions.note: Do not withhold needed oxygen in hypoxaemia. Evidence for a precise FiO₂ limit decades after bleomycin is uncertain.

questions.stem: The muscle or muscle group with the greatest resistance to the action of non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents is the

opts.why: Upper-airway/pharyngeal muscles are relatively sensitive, particularly to residual blockade.
Adductor pollicis is relatively sensitive and useful for monitoring recovery, unlike the diaphragm.
Laryngeal adductors are relatively resistant but the diaphragm is the strongest conventional answer in this set.

questions.expl: The diaphragm is relatively resistant to non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking drugs, requiring a higher concentration for equivalent blockade. Adductor pollicis is more sensitive, making it useful for recovery monitoring but not diaphragmatic onset.
