questions.stem: A patient presents for a trans-urethral resection of the prostate (TURP). He had a single drug- eluting coronary stent for angina pectoris inserted six months ago and is taking clopidogrel and aspirin. The most appropriate preoperative management of his medications is to

opts.t: Continue both antiplatelet agents without discussion
opts.why: Continuing both agents regardless of surgical bleeding risk ignores individualised cardiology/surgery assessment.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant, not a substitute for stent-protective platelet inhibition.

opts.t: Continue aspirin and, if surgery is truly elective, defer until a safe antiplatelet interval is established
Stop both aspirin and clopidogrel seven days before every case
opts.why: Stopping both drugs risks stent thrombosis; aspirin continuation and timing must be considered.

questions.expl: Following drug-eluting stent placement, stopping dual antiplatelet therapy prematurely carries stent-thrombosis risk. Decisions at six months require urgency, bleeding risk and cardiology input. Aspirin is often continued when possible; clopidogrel management is individualised.
questions.note: Period-specific guidelines differed on ideal delay after DES; this reconstruction deliberately avoids a single unconditional clopidogrel rule.

questions.stem: A ten year old child (weight 30 kg) presents to the emergency department in status epilepticus. He has received one dose of 15 mg midazolam buccally prior to his arrival. According to Advanced Paediatric Life Supprt, Australia (APLS) guidelines the next drug treatment should be intravenous

opts.why: Morphine does not terminate status epilepticus.

opts.t: Immediate high-dose propofol without airway plan
opts.why: Propofol without airway preparation is not the routine next step after one prehospital benzodiazepine dose.

opts.t: Oral sodium valproate as the sole urgent intervention
opts.why: Oral valproate has delayed onset and is not an adequate sole treatment for ongoing convulsive status.

opts.t: A second appropriately dosed benzodiazepine, such as IV midazolam, if still seizing

questions.expl: Paediatric status epilepticus protocols allow a second benzodiazepine after the first prehospital dose before second-line antiseizure agents. For a 30-kg child the IV midazolam dose is weight-based and local protocol-dependent.
questions.note: The Anki recall states IV midazolam; use contemporary local dose and step timing rather than the older recalled fixed dose.

questions.stem: A peripheral intravenous cannula is being inserted in the forearm of a man having a hemicolectomy. The skin asepsis preparation NOT suitable for this procedure is

opts.why: Licensed skin antisepsis is appropriate before peripheral IV placement.
70% isopropanol provides acceptable skin antisepsis when used appropriately.

opts.t: Chlorhexidine in alcohol appropriate for vascular access
opts.why: Chlorhexidine-alcohol preparations are standard vascular-access skin-prep choices.

questions.expl: Peripheral IV insertion requires an approved antiseptic skin preparation and drying time. Household detergent is not a procedural skin antiseptic. Chlorhexidine–alcohol or alcohol-based products are routinely used subject to allergy and age.
questions.note: The original candidate preparations were not available; reconstructed exception is unequivocal but not authenticated.

questions.stem: In pulmonary function testing the presence of airflow limitation is defined by a post- bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than

opts.why: A ratio below 1.0 would label nearly everyone obstructed and lacks specificity.

opts.t: Less than 0.50 after bronchodilator as the definition
opts.why: A 0.50 cut-off is much lower than the GOLD definition and misses milder obstruction.
A pre-bronchodilator threshold of 0.90 is neither the criterion nor the correct timing.

questions.expl: The standard GOLD spirometric criterion confirming persistent airflow obstruction is post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70. Values of FEV1 percent predicted stage severity, rather than define obstruction.
questions.note: Fixed ratio may overdiagnose older people and underdiagnose some younger people; LLN is an alternative interpretive approach.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with morbid obesity (body mass index [BMI] 55 kg/m2) presents for middle ear surgery. The most appropriate bolus dose of propofol for induction should be based on

opts.t: Lean body weight rather than actual total body weight
Age alone without regard to body composition
opts.why: Age alone does not account for distribution volume, haemodynamics and drug response.
Twice ideal body weight can overshoot lean mass and overdose a propofol induction bolus.
Unadjusted total body weight risks excessive drug exposure in severe obesity.

questions.expl: For induction boluses in obesity, propofol pharmacokinetic dosing is often scaled to lean or adjusted body weight and titrated to effect, since total body weight can substantially overdose the patient.
questions.note: Dosing strategy depends on age and haemodynamics; reconstructed exam-style comparison.

questions.stem: A 30 year old athlete undergoing a knee arthroscopy under general anaesthesia becomes tachycardic intraoperatively. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is obtained. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: VF is chaotic and has no orderly narrow regular QRS complexes.

opts.t: Complete heart block with profound bradycardia
opts.why: Complete heart block generally gives AV dissociation and a slower escape rhythm, unlike SVT.
Asystole lacks organised ventricular complexes and cannot explain a rapid regular tachycardia.

questions.expl: The practice ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia consistent with SVT. Distinguish from ventricular fibrillation (chaotic), asystole (no rhythm) and complete heart block (usually a slower escape rhythm).
questions.note: The original 12-lead ECG was not published and the precise original rhythm cannot be authenticated. Replacement example tests an identifiable mechanism.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has the following results on his blood biochemistry testing: (Liver Function Tests shown). The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: ALP/GGT elevation is incompatible with entirely normal liver enzymes.

opts.t: Cholestatic liver-enzyme pattern with predominantly elevated ALP and GGT
Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes
opts.why: Isolated unconjugated bilirubin with normal enzymes does not match the cholestatic enzyme rise.
Predominant ALT elevation indicates hepatocellular injury rather than biliary cholestasis.

questions.expl: A cholestatic pattern is characterised by disproportionate ALP/GGT rise versus transaminases; a hepatocellular pattern has prominent ALT/AST elevations. The original biochemical table is missing, so a reconstructed table is supplied.
questions.note: Reconstructed example; the original 2021.2 diagnosis cannot be known from the published stem alone.

questions.stem: The Vortex Approach to airway management does all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Optimising tracheal intubation is a Vortex upper-airway lifeline.
Face-mask oxygenation is one of the three Vortex lifelines.
Supraglottic airway oxygenation is another lifeline; teams may move between them.

opts.t: The Vortex approach is a strict, mandatory sequence requiring exhausting intubation before other lifelines

questions.expl: The Vortex cognitive aid allows movement between three upper-airway lifelines, each optimised using appropriate adjuncts, with escalation to emergency front-of-neck access if oxygenation cannot be restored. It is not a rigid sequential algorithm.

questions.stem: A structure that is NOT clamped during a Pringle manoeuvre is the

opts.t: Bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament
opts.why: Bile duct is in the portal triad compressed in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
Proper hepatic artery is clamped as part of portal inflow.
Portal vein is clamped and its hepatic inflow interrupted.

questions.expl: The Pringle manoeuvre clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament including portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct; the hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC and are not included.

questions.stem: A forest plot is a commonly used tool in meta-analysis. It presents

opts.t: Effect estimates and confidence intervals for individual studies and the pooled effect

opts.why: A forest plot contains effect sizes and confidence intervals, not simply participant ages.

opts.t: Only the p values without sample sizes
opts.why: Individual study effect estimates, not only bare p-values, are displayed.

opts.t: The raw individual-patient data of each study
opts.why: Patient-level raw data are not conventionally plotted; study-level effect estimates are.

questions.expl: A forest plot shows individual study effect measures with confidence intervals, study weights and often a pooled estimate, allowing visual assessment of consistency/heterogeneity.

questions.stem: Of the following, the procedure that is most commonly associated with chronic pain after surgery is

opts.why: Routine laparoscopic cholecystectomy has a lower chronic-pain prevalence than major amputation.
Uncomplicated cataract surgery rarely causes persistent severe postsurgical pain.
Diagnostic gastroscopy generally does not involve the tissue/nerve injury of amputation.

questions.expl: Post-amputation persistent pain and phantom limb pain are common, with higher proportions than after routine minor laparoscopic or ophthalmic procedures.

questions.stem: Performing a superficial cervical plexus block will block all of the following nerves EXCEPT the

opts.why: Transverse cervical nerve is a superficial C2–C3 ventral cervical plexus branch.
Great auricular nerve belongs to the superficial cervical plexus.
Lesser occipital nerve is a superficial C2 ventral-ramus plexus branch; greater occipital is dorsal.

questions.expl: Superficial cervical plexus block targets C2–C4 ventral branches: lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves. Greater occipital is a dorsal ramus and lies outside the superficial plexus.

questions.stem: Suxamethonium causes a sustained contraction of the extraocular muscles for up to

opts.why: Twenty-four hours is vastly longer than the reported transient extraocular contraction effect.
Two hours markedly exceeds the short-lived suxamethonium effect.
One second is too brief to cover the transient extraocular contraction/IOP change.

questions.expl: Suxamethonium can cause a transient rise in intraocular pressure and extraocular muscle effects; older physiological reports cite a period up to around 20 minutes for changes in muscle tension. The effects vary and are not a universal constant.
questions.note: Historical recalled numerical value, not a guideline interval for eye surgery.

questions.stem: Findings associated with massive pericardial tamponade include

opts.t: An obligatory normal jugular venous pressure
opts.why: Raised, not necessarily normal, JVP is expected from pericardial filling restriction.
The pathology is an increase in intrapericardial pressure, which impairs filling.

opts.t: Raised central venous pressure with reduced cardiac output and pulsus paradoxus

opts.why: Stroke volume falls when cardiac filling is externally compressed; it does not universally rise.

questions.expl: Tamponade impairs diastolic filling, typically causing raised venous pressure, impaired output and respiratory variation in systolic pressure. Tachycardia is usual; bradycardia is not a classic early sign.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old lady presents for elective coronary artery graft surgery. She has a pulmonary artery catheter inserted with the waveforms displayed below. Her cardiac output is 4.5 L/min. Her mean pulmonary artery pressure is 33 mmHg. The most likely explanation for the waveforms seen is that she has

opts.t: Normal right atrial and pulmonary artery pressures
opts.why: Prominent systolic RA waves and altered pulmonary pressures do not fit wholly normal right-sided pressures.
Aortic stenosis is a left outflow valve lesion and does not create the characteristic RA v-wave contour.

opts.t: A normal pulmonary artery waveform with no haemodynamic pathology
opts.why: An entirely normal PA/RA waveform conflicts with the large RA systolic regurgitant waves.

opts.t: Severe tricuspid regurgitation with prominent right-atrial systolic v waves

questions.expl: A pulmonary-artery-catheter tracing with large right-atrial systolic waves and an elevated mPAP may indicate tricuspid regurgitation, though other causes depend on the full catheter waveform. CO 4.5 L/min alone does not establish TR.
questions.note: Original pressure tracings unavailable; a representative right-heart waveform is used. Original clinical diagnosis remains uncertain without the trace.

questions.stem: A patient with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and chronic obstructive airways disease develops a wheeze intraoperatively which resolves with administration of salbutamol via the endotracheal tube. Soon after, he develops rapid atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 120 beats per minute, a BP of 90/60 and an ETCO2 of 40mmHg. His regular medications are inhaled salbutamol, inhaled salmeterol and digoxin 125mcg daily. The next most suitable treatment is

opts.t: Routine large esmolol bolus during active bronchospasm
opts.why: Esmolol may provoke bronchoconstriction or hypotension in this borderline patient.

opts.t: Repeated IV salbutamol to increase rate
opts.why: Additional salbutamol can worsen tachyarrhythmia without addressing AF.

opts.t: Intravenous amiodarone following assessment of stability
Immediate low-energy unsynchronised shock in a perfusing patient
opts.why: Unsynchronised shock is for VF/pulseless VT, not a perfusing patient with AF.

questions.expl: For atrial fibrillation during bronchospasm with borderline haemodynamics, amiodarone may provide rate or rhythm control when beta-blockers are unattractive. Haemodynamic instability requiring immediate cardioversion must be assessed; this patient has preserved CO₂ and a blood pressure of 90/60.
questions.note: 2021.2-specific Brainscape recall favours amiodarone. The safest actual treatment depends on stability and reversible triggers.

questions.stem: A man with atrial fibrillation has no valvular heart disease. According to joint American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC) and Heart Rhythm Society (HRS) guidelines, oral anticoagulants are definitely recommended if his CHA2DS2-VASc score is greater than or equal to

opts.t: Score four as the minimum in every patient
opts.why: Four is not the minimum for anticoagulation in every patient; risk thresholds start lower.
Score zero does not mandate anticoagulation under the cited guidance.

opts.t: Score one as a universal strong indication
opts.why: A score of one in men generally prompts consideration, not a universal Class I recommendation.

opts.t: CHA₂DS₂-VASc score at least two in a man

questions.expl: The 2019 AHA/ACC/HRS focused update supports oral anticoagulation at CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women (without relevant contraindications). Score one in men usually prompts consideration rather than a universal requirement.

questions.stem: The advantage of the Mapleson E circuit in paediatric anaesthesia is due to its

opts.why: Mapleson E is a low-resistance circuit, not a high-resistance system.
There is no built-in ventilator bellows in a simple Ayre T-piece.
No CO₂ absorber is present; adequate fresh-gas flow prevents rebreathing.

opts.t: Low circuit resistance and minimal apparatus dead space

questions.expl: The Ayre T-piece or Mapleson E system has very low resistance and little dead space, advantageous in small children; it requires appropriate high fresh-gas flows for spontaneous ventilation.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has the following pulmonary function test result: (Results displayed) The diagnosis is most consistent with

opts.t: Uncomplicated asthma with a normal DLCO
opts.why: Uncomplicated asthma often has normal or elevated DLCO and obstructive, not preserved-ratio isolated low-transfer, physiology.

opts.t: Pulmonary vascular disease, such as pulmonary embolism
A normal healthy lung function test
opts.why: The low DLCO is abnormal and excludes normal PFT interpretation.

opts.t: Pure restrictive obesity with preserved transfer factor
opts.why: Simple obesity may restrict volumes but often preserves the transfer factor; isolated low DLCO suggests vascular disease.

questions.expl: A preserved spirometric ratio with reduced DLCO can point to pulmonary vascular pathology, including PE or pulmonary hypertension. The reconstructed PFT table demonstrates this pattern.
questions.note: Original PFT data absent; the practice table is an illustrative replacement rather than an authenticated original diagnosis.

questions.stem: When performing a paediatric pain assessment, the five elements assessed to obtain the FLACC score are

opts.t: Facial expression, lung sounds, airway, consciousness, circulation
opts.why: This set combines unrelated clinical observations rather than FLACC pain domains.
The letters here have no relationship to the validated behavioural pain score.

opts.t: Fatigue, limb circumference, appetite, cognition, colour
opts.why: These measures are neither the named FLACC domains nor a validated infant behavioural pain scale.

questions.expl: FLACC is an observational paediatric pain scale scoring Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability on a 0–2 scale each, total 0–10.

questions.stem: Local anaesthetic blockade of the sciatic nerve results in loss of function of all of the following EXCEPT

opts.t: Knee extension supplied by the femoral nerve
Ankle dorsiflexion through the common fibular division
opts.why: Sciatic/common fibular innervation controls dorsiflexion, so blockade may weaken it.
Tibial division of sciatic innervates ankle plantar flexors.
Sciatic branches supply hamstrings responsible for knee flexion.

questions.expl: Sciatic nerve blockade impairs hamstrings and most motor function distal to the knee, but quadriceps-mediated knee extension is femoral-nerve territory.

questions.stem: Methylene blue may be used in the treatment of all of the following conditions EXCEPT

opts.why: Methylene blue is used in selected refractory vasoplegic states.

opts.t: Treatment of methaemoglobinaemia in a patient with G6PD deficiency
Treatment of methemoglobinaemia without G6PD deficiency
opts.why: Methylene blue is standard antidotal therapy for methemoglobinaemia with intact NADPH function.
Ifosfamide-associated encephalopathy is a recognised off-label use in selected cases.

questions.expl: Methylene blue may be used for methaemoglobinaemia, refractory vasoplegia or selected toxic syndromes. In G6PD deficiency its effect is impaired and it can cause haemolysis, making it unsafe.

questions.stem: A respiratory effect of high flow nasal oxygen therapy is

opts.t: Reduced respiratory rate for a given minute ventilation

opts.why: High-flow oxygen does not protect against regurgitation/aspiration.

opts.t: Consistent severe respiratory depression in all patients
opts.why: HFNO commonly reduces work of breathing, not invariably causes major respiratory depression.

opts.t: Universal alveolar hyperventilation independent of flow
opts.why: Alveolar ventilation depends on patient effort and physiology; it is not universally increased independent of flow.

questions.expl: High-flow nasal oxygen can wash out pharyngeal dead space, improve end-expiratory lung volume and reduce work of breathing; spontaneous RR may fall without reducing effective alveolar ventilation.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has ROTEM results including (results displayed) . The most appropriate treatment is

opts.t: Platelet deficiency or dysfunction suggested by low EXTEM firmness with preserved FIBTEM

opts.why: APTEM correction of rapid lysis suggests hyperfibrinolysis and points toward antifibrinolytic therapy.
A near-flat FIBTEM suggests inadequate fibrinogen rather than isolated platelet dysfunction.
HEPTEM correction of INTEM prolongation suggests heparin effect, not platelet failure.

questions.expl: When FIBTEM clot firmness is preserved but EXTEM maximum clot firmness is reduced, the platelet contribution is impaired; transfusing platelets may be appropriate in a bleeding patient. The alternative ROTEM patterns guide fibrinogen replacement, TXA or heparin reversal.
questions.note: Practice reconstruction follows the recalled ROTEM pattern. The original 2021.2 trace is unavailable; this cannot authenticate the exam key.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate contains all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Fibrinogen is the dominant intended coagulation protein in cryoprecipitate.
VWF is present in cryoprecipitate along with factor VIII.

opts.t: Factor IX as a factor not concentrated in cryoprecipitate

opts.why: Factor VIII is enriched in cryoprecipitate; it is factor IX that is not concentrated.

questions.expl: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, vWF, factor VIII, factor XIII and fibronectin, but not meaningful concentrated factor IX, which is a vitamin-K-dependent factor.
questions.note: Original answer options missing; factor IX is a correct representative EXCEPT choice.

questions.stem: The size 5 i-gel® supraglottic airway is recommended for patients who weigh over

opts.why: 35 kg corresponds to a smaller i-gel size, not size 5.
25 kg is below large-adult size-5 manufacturer's guidance.
50 kg often falls within size-4 rather than size-5 recommendation.

questions.expl: Manufacturer size guidance specifies i-gel size 5 for large adults over 90 kg. Size 4 generally serves 50–90 kg and smaller sizes suit lighter patients.

questions.stem: A normal 75 kg term parturient may be expected to have a total blood volume of

opts.why: Three litres is substantially below the term-parturient expanded blood-volume estimate.
11.5 litres is above a reasonable 75-kg term-parturient estimate.
Five litres approximates a nonpregnant adult blood volume and ignores gestational expansion.

questions.expl: Term pregnancy increases maternal blood volume around 40–50%; the recalled exam estimate uses roughly 100 mL/kg at 75 kg, giving 7.5 L, though actual volumes vary considerably.
questions.note: A 75-kg person's predicted volume and percentage increase vary by lean mass and baseline size.

questions.stem: The nerve labelled by the arrow in the diagram below is the

opts.why: Obturator nerve emerges at the medial edge of psoas and runs toward obturator foramen, not on anterior psoas.
Femoral nerve emerges lateral to psoas and passes under the inguinal ligament.

opts.t: Genitofemoral nerve on the reconstructed lumbar plexus figure

opts.why: Iliohypogastric nerve travels laterally across quadratus lumborum, not descending on psoas anterior surface.

questions.expl: The genitofemoral nerve emerges through the anterior surface of psoas and descends on the muscle. Femoral and obturator nerves travel along different paths; the iliohypogastric runs laterally across quadratus lumborum.
questions.note: The original 2021.2 diagram was not published. Reconstructed lumbar-plexus figure is a representative exercise, not a verified arrow identification.

questions.stem: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx do NOT include

opts.why: Lateral cricoarytenoid adducts vocal cords and is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the intrinsic sole vocal-fold abductor.
Thyroarytenoid alters vocal-fold tension and is intrinsic.

questions.expl: The omohyoid is an extrinsic infrahyoid strap muscle. The intrinsic laryngeal muscles move the vocal folds and cartilages and include cricoarytenoids and thyroarytenoid.

questions.stem: Of the following, the deficit that DOES NOT result from damage to the common peroneal nerve is

opts.why: Foot drop results from weak common fibular-innervated dorsiflexors.

opts.t: Loss of knee extension as a deficit not caused by isolated common peroneal nerve damage
Loss of sensation over lateral shin and dorsum of foot
opts.why: Lateral shin/dorsal-foot sensory loss fits common fibular nerve injury.
Weak ankle eversion results from superficial fibular nerve branch injury.

questions.expl: The common fibular nerve supplies dorsiflexion, eversion and superficial/dorsal-foot sensory territory. Knee extension is provided by femoral nerve via quadriceps.
questions.note: An Anki summary inconsistently listed foot drop in an 'EXCEPT' context; foot drop is a classic peroneal lesion manifestation, so the answer is corrected.

questions.stem: A patient has numbness and weakness in her hand postoperatively. You are trying to distinguish between an ulnar nerve lesion and a C8-T1 radiculopathy. You can diagnose a C8-T1 radiculopathy if she has weakness

opts.why: Thumb adduction is ulnar-innervated and can be weak in isolated ulnar palsy.
Interossei are ulnar-innervated and do not distinguish root from isolated nerve injury.
Little-finger abductor is ulnar-innervated and weak in either lesion.

opts.t: Weakness of thumb abduction (abductor pollicis brevis)

questions.expl: Abductor pollicis brevis is median-innervated but C8–T1 supplied, so weakness suggests root or lower-plexus lesion beyond isolated ulnar neuropathy. Ulnar intrinsic muscle weakness alone cannot distinguish these disorders.

questions.stem: The domains described in the Edmonton Frail Scale do NOT include

opts.why: Medication usage is an Edmonton Frail Scale category.
Social support is explicitly assessed.
Cognition forms a separate frailty domain.

opts.t: Chronological age as a scoring item

questions.expl: The Edmonton Frail Scale covers cognition, general health, functional independence, social support, medication, nutrition, mood, continence and functional performance. Chronological age is not an independent scored domain.

questions.stem: In a patient with anaemia of chronic disease, of the following the most likely to be elevated is

opts.why: Transferrin is often low or normal as a negative acute-phase reactant.
Inflammatory iron sequestration lowers serum iron rather than increasing it.
Transferrin saturation is typically reduced because circulating available iron falls.

questions.expl: Anaemia of chronic inflammation involves hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration, low serum iron and often low transferrin saturation, with normal or elevated ferritin as an acute-phase reactant.

questions.stem: The equipment shown in the picture below is a

opts.why: Arndt blocker provides endobronchial occlusion, not laryngeal EMG contact electrodes.
A standard single-lumen ETT lacks the surface electrodes of a nerve-monitoring tube.
Cohen blocker has steerable endobronchial occlusion apparatus, not monitoring electrode bands.

questions.expl: A NIM endotracheal tube has exposed surface electrodes designed to contact the vocal cords, allowing recurrent laryngeal nerve EMG monitoring. Bronchial blockers provide lung isolation and lack laryngeal electrodes.

questions.stem: The estimated proportion of human induced climate change attributable to nitrous oxide is

opts.why: 0.06% is orders of magnitude below the recalled contribution of total anthropogenic N₂O.
0.006% grossly understates N₂O's greenhouse contribution.
60% grossly overstates nitrous oxide's share of human-induced climate forcing.

questions.expl: Older examination reading approximated nitrous oxide's contribution to anthropogenic climate forcing as around 6%; this refers to all sources of N₂O, not the tiny subset from anaesthetic use.
questions.note: Older estimates and attribution conventions differ from current greenhouse-gas accounting; this is a historical recalled figure.
